anchor: Wave quantities and phase > The wave channel of 1825: "Illuminated from behind, the amber particles revealed the hidden internal motion of the fluid."
purpose: Illustrate the Weber brothers' 1825 wave channel experiment showing water wave propagation, comparing the advancing surface profile with the localized cyclic motion of suspended amber particles at sequentially delayed stages of oscillation.
what_to_show: A longitudinal side-view schematic of the 1825 Weber wave channel. The glass canal has transparent walls showing water with a wavy surface profile travelling from left to right, indicated by a green horizontal arrow labelled 'wave propagation'. Beneath the surface, three suspended amber particles are highlighted at different horizontal positions. Circular or elliptical dashed orbit paths with directional arrows show localized cyclic motion around equilibrium for each particle. Annotation indicates 'Amber particles execute local closed cycles without net forward drift'. Sequentially delayed particle positions demonstrate phase difference along the canal.
what_to_notice: While the wave crest travels horizontally along the entire channel, each individual amber particle stays in its local region, oscillating about its resting equilibrium position.

anchor: Wave quantities and phase > Displacement and amplitude: "A progressive wave creates a repeating pattern of peaks and troughs across space."
purpose: Define instantaneous displacement, amplitude, and wavelength on a spatial snapshot of a progressive wave at a fixed time t0.
what_to_show: A scientific coordinate plot showing vertical displacement y against horizontal distance x for a transverse wave snapshot at fixed time t0. A horizontal dashed centre line marks equilibrium y = 0. A vertical double-headed green arrow from the equilibrium line to a crest is labelled 'amplitude A'. A vertical signed vector arrow from the equilibrium line to a point on the wave is labelled 'displacement y'. Horizontal dimension lines label 'wavelength lambda' between adjacent crests and between adjacent troughs. An explicit crossed-out red dimension line from crest to trough is labelled 'peak-to-peak = 2A (not amplitude)'.
what_to_notice: Amplitude A is strictly measured from the equilibrium centre line to a peak or trough. Peak-to-peak distance is twice the amplitude.

anchor: Wave quantities and phase > Period and frequency: "A displacement-time graph tracks the movement of one medium particle as time passes."
purpose: Define period T and frequency f on a temporal displacement-time graph for a single oscillating medium particle at a fixed position x0.
what_to_show: A plot showing vertical displacement y against time t for a single oscillating particle at a fixed position x0. A horizontal dashed line indicates equilibrium y = 0. A horizontal dimension line between two consecutive peaks is labelled 'period T (time for one complete cycle)'. A vertical dimension line from the equilibrium line to a peak is labelled 'amplitude A'. A side callout box displays the reciprocal relationship 'f = 1 / T' with annotation 'frequency f = cycles per unit time (Hz)'.
what_to_notice: The horizontal axis represents time t, so the horizontal distance across one full repeating wave cycle gives the period T, not the wavelength.

anchor: Wave quantities and phase > Reading wave graphs: space versus time: "A displacement-distance graph captures a frozen snapshot of the wave at one instant in time."
purpose: Provide authentic Cambridge Paper 2 evidence showing how examiners test extraction of wavelength and calculation of phase difference between two points on a spatial displacement-distance grid.
what_to_show: Authentic examination figure from Cambridge paper 9702/22/F/M/16 Question 4 Fig. 4.2 showing a damped sinusoidal wave of vertical displacement y / cm against distance x / cm from x = 0 to 11 cm, with major grid lines every 2 cm and subdivisions of 0.2 cm. Waveform crosses equilibrium at x = 1.0, 3.0, 5.0, 7.0, 9.0 cm, with crests at x = 2.0, 6.0, 10.0 cm.
what_to_notice: Because the horizontal axis represents distance x / cm, the horizontal separation between adjacent crests (from x = 2.0 cm to x = 6.0 cm) gives the wavelength lambda = 4.0 cm. Liquid particles at x = 3.0 cm and x = 4.0 cm have separation Delta x = 1.0 cm, giving a phase difference of (1.0 / 4.0) x 360 degrees = 90 degrees.

anchor: Wave quantities and phase > Quantitative phase difference: "Two waves can share the same frequency but reach their peaks at different times."
purpose: Provide authentic Cambridge Paper 2 evidence showing two progressive waves R and S on the same displacement-time axes for an oscillating particle to determine period, amplitudes, time shift, and phase difference.
what_to_show: Authentic examination figure from Cambridge paper 9702/23/M/J/16 Question 7 Fig. 7.2 displaying displacement x / cm against time t / s for two sinusoidal waves R and S. Wave R has amplitude 3.4 cm and crest at t = 0.15 s. Wave S has amplitude 2.2 cm and crest at t = 0.25 s. Both waves have period T = 0.60 s.
what_to_notice: Both waves share the same repeating period T = 0.60 s. The crest of wave S occurs 0.10 s after the crest of wave R. This time shift Delta t = 0.10 s yields a phase difference of (0.10 s / 0.60 s) x 360 degrees = 60 degrees (or pi/3 rad).

anchor: Wave quantities and phase > What is phase?: "Particles with identical displacement can move in opposite directions at the same instant."
purpose: Resolve the misconception that equal displacement proves equal phase by linking wave profile points to a reference phase circle (0 to 360 degrees and 0 to 2 pi radians), showing that points with equal displacement can move in opposite directions.
what_to_show: A dual-panel diagram pairing a reference phase circle on the left with a sinusoidal wave profile on the right. Left panel: a unit circle with angles marked at 0 degrees, 90 degrees (top), 180 degrees (left), 270 degrees (bottom), and 360 degrees. A rotating phasor indicates phase angle phi. Right panel: a sinusoidal wave with four highlighted points. Point A is at equilibrium (y = 0) moving upward (phase 0 degrees). Point B is at positive peak (+A, phase 90 degrees). Point C is at equilibrium (y = 0) moving downward (phase 180 degrees). Point D is at negative trough (-A, phase 270 degrees). Points A and C both have y = 0, but opposite velocity arrows emphasize that they are in antiphase (180 degrees apart).
what_to_notice: Points A and C have the exact same displacement (y = 0) but opposite velocity directions. Equal displacement alone does not mean two points are in phase.

anchor: Wave quantities and phase > Reading wave graphs: space versus time: "Points separated by one full cycle on a displacement-time graph mark one period."
purpose: Provide authentic Cambridge Paper 1 evidence showing how examiners assess the discrimination between horizontal time period and vertical displacement on a displacement-time curve.
what_to_show: Authentic examination figure from Cambridge paper 9702/11/M/J/18 Question 20 showing a sinusoidal displacement against time graph for a single point on a string. Two points X and Y on consecutive cycles have equal positive displacement and both lie on downward-sloping sections, connected by a horizontal dashed line.
what_to_notice: Because the horizontal axis is time, the separation XY between identical cycle stages represents the time period of the wave, while the vertical position of points X and Y indicates equal instantaneous displacement.
